papers.title: Cost-Effectiveness of a Child and Parent Mindfulness-Based Training Versus Medication for Childhood ADHD.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: ADHD imposes substantial societal costs. This randomized controlled trial examined the cost-effectiveness of family mindfulness training ("MYmind") versus medication in childhood ADHD. METHOD: An economic evaluation with a 10-month time horizon was conducted from a societal perspective. Children ( RESULTS: At 10 months, primary cost-effectiveness analyses indicated that MYmind was inferior to medication for inattention but had higher QALY gains at higher costs. Specifically, MYmind had a 27% probability of being cost-effective for inattention and a 30% probability for QALYs. Secondary analyses showed similar results with even lower chances for mindfulness being cost-effective in the shorter-term horizons. Notably, in the subgroup excluding crossover participants, MYmind was dominant over medication, with an 81% chance to be cost-effective for both outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: MYmind was less cost-effective than medication in the short and medium term. Long-term cost-effectiveness of MYmind remained low for the total group, but was high among participants who did not crossover to the alternative treatment.

papers.title: Emotional awareness moderates the relationship between emotion recognition and emotion regulation: Exploratory and confirmatory evidence.
papers.abstract: Effective emotion regulation plays a critical role in mental health. Identifying factors that contribute to this ability could have clinical relevance. Two candidate factors are emotion recognition and emotional awareness. Specifically, if one does not recognize emotions in the self or others-and does not have a fine-grained understanding (trait awareness) of those emotions-it may be difficult to identify effective regulation strategies. papers.title: Emotion Regulation is Associated with Symptoms of Racial Trauma Among Minoritized People.
papers.abstract: Race-based traumatic stress (RBTS) can develop after prolonged exposure to racial discrimination and shares similar symptoms to post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). However, there is a scarcity of research investigating specific psychological processes associated with RBTS that may inform intervention development. As PTSD and RBTS have shared symptomology, it is possible that psychological processes implicated in PTSD may also be implicated in RBTS. papers.title: Evaluation of interdisciplinary child exploitation training for children's nursing students.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Child exploitation is a significant safeguarding concern and nurses have a crucial role in recognising and responding to it. Therefore, it is essential that children's nursing students are equipped with the knowledge, confidence and preparedness to recognise and act on safeguarding concerns. AIM: To evaluate the effectiveness of a police-led child exploitation awareness training session in enhancing children's nursing students' knowledge, confidence and application of safeguarding principles in practice. METHOD: A mixed-methods study design was used. Second-year children's nursing students ( n =35) attended a three-hour police-led child exploitation awareness training session. Quantitative data were collected via a pre-training ( n =35) and post-training ( n =30) questionnaire and analysed to assess changes in three domains: knowledge and confidence; attitudes and beliefs; and willingness to act. Qualitative data were collected through follow-up forms that explored participants' ( n =8) reflections on application of their learning in their practice placements and analysed using content analysis. FINDINGS: Significant improvements were identified across all three domains, with the greatest increases in participants' confidence and escalation of concerns. Qualitative findings indicated that the participants developed enhanced professional curiosity and increased willingness to act in safeguarding situations, suggesting the effective translation of learning into practice. CONCLUSION: Practice-oriented, interdisciplinary safeguarding education can improve children's nursing students' knowledge, confidence and behavioural readiness. Such interventions may enhance nurses' ability to recognise and respond to instances of child exploitation, thereby strengthening safeguarding practice.

papers.title: Learning to self-soothe, feel safe, and be connected: participant perspectives of a mindful self-compassion program for people with multiple sclerosis.
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: People with multiple sclerosis (PwMS) often experience high rates of stress, anxiety, and depression, with low quality of life. Mindful self-compassion (MSC) training may offer a promising approach to support mental health in this population. This study explored the experiences of PwMS participating in an online MSC course as part of a feasibility trial to assess its accessibility, perceived effects, and suggested areas for improvement. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Qualitative interpretive methods were used. Semi-structured Zoom interviews were completed with 17 PwMS and three MSC facilitators after the course. Transcripts underwent reflexive thematic analysis by a team of researchers. RESULTS: Four themes were constructed: (1) "the ticking time bomb": motivations for mindful self-compassion, (2) navigating the MSC course: benefits, challenges, and accessibility, (3) a community of trust: finding support and common humanity, and (4) wishing for more: filling the gap in MS care. CONCLUSIONS: PwMS found MSC to be a meaningful and acceptable intervention that supported emotional well-being, social connection, and daily coping. MSC may complement standard MS care by addressing psychosocial needs that are often overlooked. Tailored delivery and long-term accessibility could enhance its integration into supportive care pathways.
